subject: sea spider
title: This Animal Keeps Its Guts in Its Legs, and Its Gut Is Also Its Heart

scenes.text: This animal keeps its guts in its legs. On purpose.
Sea spiders. More than 1,300 species, from a millimeter across to 70 centimeters in the cold Antarctic deep.
The body is so thin there's no room inside. So the digestive tract runs down every leg, right to the tip.
It has no gills and no lungs. Oxygen just seeps in through the legs. And its heart is too weak to push blood that far.
In 2017, scientists at McMurdo Station found the trick. The gut squeezes in waves, far harder than digestion needs, and pumps the blood instead.
Its intestines are its heart. Guts in the legs, after all.

description:
A sea spider's digestive tract runs down every one of its legs, and it uses those guts as a heart.
There are over 1,300 species of sea spiders, from a millimeter to a 70 cm leg span in Antarctic waters. Their bodies are so narrow that the gut extends into the legs, and they have no gills or lungs: oxygen diffuses in through the leg cuticle. A 2017 Current Biology study from McMurdo Station found that the heart only serves the trunk, while vigorous waves of gut contraction move blood and oxygen around the body.
What's the strangest body plan you know of in nature?
first_comment: Sea spiders aren't true spiders; they eat by pushing a straw-like proboscis into soft animals like sea anemones, which usually survive it. Which deep-sea animal should we cover next?
